title: VC0-02456
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated February 24, 2020, rejecting their claims for protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant), and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Minor Associate Appellant) are citizens of Mexico. They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated February 24, 2020, rejecting their claims for protection. The Appellants allege that they face a serious possibility of persecution at the hands of the Sinaloa drug cartel. The RPD found that the Appellants were credible but found that they had a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Mérida, or Campeche City, and dismissed their claims.
For the reasons that follow, I find that the Appellants do not have a viable IFA and substitute a decision that they are Convention refugees.

The Appellants allege that the Principal Appellant's father was an activist who vocally opposed the drug cartels operating in Mexico. The Appellants allege that as a result of the this, the Principal Appellant's brother was kidnapped, tortured and ultimately murdered. The Appellants allege that the murder was orchestrated by the Sinaloa cartel. The Appellants allege that they were followed and began receiving threats. They allege that the Principal Appellant began a crusade to try and bring the perpetrators to justice, by pressuring the state prosecutor, the human rights prosecutor, the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the XXXX of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and the XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Appellants allege that less than 36 hours later, they received threats indicating that their agents of persecution knew that the Principal Appellant had gone to the authorities. The Appellants allege that they feared for their safety and made arrangements to leave Mexico for Canada.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which, in particular cases, attracts deference. Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.1 ANALYSIS Appellants' arguments
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: The Appellants, who are self represented, argue that the RPD erred in its assessment of their forward-looking risk. They argue that the RPD failed to consider that the cartels have targeted and killed children in Mexico. They argue that their new evidence demonstrates that the Sinaloa cartel is active in the Yucatan peninsula, which would make their relocation to Mérida unsafe. The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to consider that they had previously relocated and were located by their agents of persecution. They also argue that their new evidence demonstrates that the cartels use other groups and networks to target people throughout Mexico, which would prevent them from safely relocating.

The Appellants also argue that their evidence indicates that the Sinaloa cartel has ties to government officials and the current Mexican government facilitates the drug trade. Finally, the Appellants also argue that the RPD failed to adequately consider the risk of gender-based violence faced by the Adult Associate Appellant. New evidence

Section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)2 sets out that an Appellant may only present evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection. Where evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4), the RAD will then go on to consider the factors affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Singh.3

The Appellants submit documents as new evidence with their appeal. The list of new evidence submitted with the appeal that post-dates the rejection of the Appellants' claims is as follows: 1. UN Mexico's article titled "UN Mexico calls to listen to the voices of women who demand equality and justice" dated March 10, 2020.7

The list of new evidence submitted which pre-dates the rejection of the Appellants' claims is as follows: 1. I note that Rule 3(3)(g) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules requires that the appellant's memorandum include, among other things, full and detailed submissions regarding: (iii) how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant27 The Appellants have failed to comply with these requirements and make no submissions about how their evidence meets the requirements of new evidence. I note that the Appellants are self-represented, which may present challenges in providing fulsome submissions. However, in the absence of any submissions about why the documents that pre-date the rejection of their claims were not submitted before that rejection, or any indication of their inability to obtain what appear to be open source documents, I find that these documents do not meet the statutory requirements of new evidence. Similarly, I find that the Appellants fail to establish how any of the undated documents meet the requirements of new evidence and therefore they are rejected.

Turning to the documents that post-date the rejection of their claims, these documents clearly post-date the rejection of the Appellant' claims. They provide new information about current conditions in Mexico, which could be relevant to the determination of whether the Appellants have an available IFA. They appear to be from credible sources, and therefore they meet the requirements of new evidence and will be considered with the appeal. The RAD will not hold an oral hearing.

While I have accepted new evidence with the appeal, I find that this evidence does not raise a serious issue with respect to the Appellants' credibility. Therefore, the conditions for an oral hearing, pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, are not met and a hearing will not be held. IFA is the determinative issue

I note that the RPD found that the Appellants' allegations were credible. The RPD found that the Appellants testimony was straightforward and consistent with the other evidence. Therefore, the RPD accepted that the events occurred as alleged. I agree with this determination. I also find that the Appellants have a nexus to the Convention given their impugned political opinion stemming from the activism of the Principal Appellant's father and the Principal Appellant's efforts to seek justice for his brother's murder. Therefore, I will focus my analysis on whether the Appellants have a viable IFA.

The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Rasaratnam:28 (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. (2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.

Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellants have an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option.29 First Prong: there a serious possibility of persecution in Mérida or Campeche City

The RPD found that the Appellants had not established that the agents of harm would have the means or motivation to find them in Mérida or Campeche City. The RPD noted that the Stratford Global Intelligence map in the National Documentation Package (NDP) indicated that the Sinaloa cartel was not present in these cities and found that they were among the safest cities in Mexico. The RPD noted that both cities were far from the Appellants' home community.

The RPD also noted that there was no indication that the agents of harm had targeted the Principal Appellant's other siblings. Further, the RPD cited the Principal Appellant's testimony that his father had not been harmed when he returned to Mexico. The RPD concluded that the Appellants' circumstances would not lead to the agents of harm being interested in tracking them throughout Mexico.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its analysis and that the Sinaloa cartel would be able to locate them throughout the country. The Appellants argue that the cartel has ties to law enforcement and government officials, which would allow them to track them throughout Mexico.

Having independently reviewed the record, I disagree with the RPD's conclusions that the Sinaloa cartel would not be motivated to track the Appellants. The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant's father had not been harmed when he returned to Mexico. While it may be true that the Principal Appellant's father has not been directly harmed, it is important to note that the evidence indicates that he lives between Mexico and the United States. It is unclear whether he has lived freely in Mexico for any significant period of time since the murder of his other son in 2018.

I also find that the apparent lack of interest in the Principal Appellant's siblings is not determinative of the Appellants' forward-looking risk. The Principal Appellant was actively seeking justice for his brother's murder and was lobbying a number of law enforcement and state officials. This activity lead to further threats against the Appellants. I find that the Principal Appellant's actions made him a target of the Sinaloa cartel. I also find that these efforts would continue to motivate the cartel to locate and harm the Appellants.

The Appellants' evidence also indicates that within 36 hours of the Principal Appellant's lobbying efforts, the Appellants received threats indicating that their agents of persecution were aware that they went to the authorities and threatening to murder the whole family and their dog. Therefore, I find that the Appellants' circumstances, including actively lobbying officials to seek justice against the cartel, would in fact lead the Sinaloa cartel to have an on-going motivation to locate the Appellants.

Turning to the Sinaloa cartel's ability to locate the Appellants in the IFA locations, I agree with the Appellants that the RPD failed to consider that the cartel had targeted the Appellants' family in various areas of Mexico. The Appellants' evidence is that the Principal Appellant's brother was murdered in Hermosillo, and the Appellants were threatened in Guadalajara. I note that while the cartel map in the NDP indicates that Hermosillo is within Sinaloa territory, Guadalajara is not.30 Therefore, the evidence indicates that the Appellants were threatened in a city that is outside of the established control of the Sinaloa cartel. I also note that the nature of the threats against the Appellants indicate that they were being followed in Guadalajara. The threats referenced observations such as what they were wearing and that they had a dog, suggesting that they were under surveillance in this city. Therefore, I find that the Appellants have credibly established that the cartel has targeted them outside of their general area of control.

The objective evidence indicates that the Sinaloa cartel is one of the largest and most important cartels in Mexico. The Sinaloa cartel has alliances with other cartels, including the Gulf cartel31 which is active in the IFA locations.32 The objective evidence also highlights that the Sinaloa cartel has been able to corrupt government and law enforcement officials, highlighting the complicity of such officials in the escape of the cartel's former leader, Guzmán, from a maximum security prison.33 I note that the Appellants were immediately threatened after approaching officials seeking that action be taken against the people who murdered the Principal Appellant's brother. This demonstrates that the agents of persecution have links to law enforcement. Further, the threats themselves say that the cartel was "the police."34 Given the ties of the agents of persecution to law enforcement, I find that they would be able to locate the Appellants throughout Mexico.
As I find that the Appellants would face a serious possibility of persecution throughout Mexico, I will not go on to consider the second prong analysis. State Protection

While the RPD did not make a determination on state protection, I am able to do so on the basis of the record before me. The objective evidence establishes that despite some efforts by the state to combat crime, the police are generally ineffective and often tainted by corruption.35 The objective evidence also sets out that due to this corruption, law enforcement in Mexico has assisted criminals and the cartels and engaged in human rights violations.36 In the Appellants' case, their agents of persecution have already demonstrated their ability to infiltrate law enforcement officials. Therefore, I find that on a balance of probabilities, state protection is not available.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are Convention refugees. (signed) J. Lourenço J. Lourenço February 24, 2020 Date 1 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v.
